steps.title: Equation → two graphs → intersection
steps.body:
Any equation can be solved by graphing:
•  left side as \(y_1\), right side as \(y_2\), exactly as written
•  find where the graphs cross: at that point \(y_1=y_2\)
•  the \(x\)-coordinate of the crossing is the solution; the \(y\)-coordinate is the common value

There can be more than one crossing. Each one is a solution; the question may ask for all of them, or only one (“for \(x>0\)”, “the larger root”).

steps.title: Which two graphs do you draw?
steps.ok: ✓ Right. Each side as written; nothing rearranged, so nothing can go wrong.
bads: ✗ The right-hand side is \(3-x\), not \(3\). Graph each side exactly as written.
✗ That rearrangement is valid, but it is a chance to make a sign error. Graph each side as written: \(y_1=\ln x\), \(y_2=3-x\).

steps.title: Equations from a context
steps.body:
A “story” is a word problem: the equation is not written for you, it is hidden in a context (two populations, cost and revenue, two temperatures). The same three moves apply, with two extras:
•  write the equation first: “equal” means \(P=Q\), so \(500e^{0.1t}=2000-80t\)
•  the \(x\)-coordinate answers “when?”; the \(y\)-coordinate answers “how many?”, so read both
•  give units, and round sensibly: \(t=9.25\) years; a population of \(1260\), not \(1260.36\)

steps.title: Domains, windows and radians
steps.body:
Three checks before you press intersect:
•  the domain in the question is your window: “for \(0\le x\le5\)” means Xmin \(0\), Xmax \(5\), and only crossings inside count
•  if the function involves \(\sin\), \(\cos\) or \(\tan\), the calculator must be in radians (IB uses radians unless degrees are written)
•  a \(y\)-range that is too small hides the crossing; too large squashes it. Use the values in the question as a guide
